title: Guest post: Greenland ice sheet shrinks for 30th year in a row - Carbon Brief
gist: DMI scientists estimate Greenland lost about 135bn tonnes of ice in the year to August 2026, or 173bn tonnes under a new observation-based method. It was the 30th straight year of net loss, even though surface mass balance was the sixth highest in 46 years. Calving, including the largest Petermann glacier break-off since 2012, and a lucky Omega-shaped jet stream pattern drove the year. The IMBIE assessment shows Greenland dominates ice-sheet sea level rise so far and warns of a 'Greenlandification' of the roughly 10x larger Antarctic ice sheet.

insights.claim: Greenland's ice sheet lost about 135bn tonnes of ice in the 12 months to August 2026, based on an average of three climate models. A new estimate that combines one model with weather stations, satellites, GPS and aircraft observations puts the loss higher, at 173bn tonnes.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The gap between the two methods shows that ice-loss estimates are structurally uncertain. The observation-based figure suggests the model-average figure understates losses.

insights.claim: Greenland's surface mass balance for 2025-26 was 519bn tonnes, the sixth highest in a 46-year dataset and about 178bn tonnes above the 1981-2010 average of roughly 350bn tonnes. Even so, the ice sheet still lost mass overall.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Net loss even in a good surface year shows that ice discharge, not weather, now sets the baseline, so the downtrend holds up against favourable years.
insights.quote: it was not an “extreme” year for weather in Greenland – and, yet, the ice sheet ended firmly in the red

insights.claim: Calving and glacier retreat have driven roughly two-thirds of Greenland's total ice loss to date. Losses at the ice sheet's edges continue apace even in years when the surface mass budget is unremarkable.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Ocean-driven dynamic loss is the dominant and less weather-dependent driver, which makes long-run sea level projections less sensitive to individual cool summers.
insights.locator: The recent breakaway is a reminder

insights.claim: An unusually dry winter and spring in southern Greenland left about 40bn tonnes less snow than normal, removing the usual protective buffer. A cool, snowy, cloudy June then delayed the melt season's onset to 5 June, nine days later than the 1981-2010 average.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Shows how much the timing of snowfall changes annual ice loss, which is a source of noise when reading single-year figures.

insights.claim: Surface melt peaked on 22 July 2026 at 74.9% of the Greenland ice sheet, below the record set in July 2025, when 81.2% was melting at once. Much of the 2026 meltwater refroze in the snowpack, keeping surface mass balance nearly flat from mid-June to mid-July.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Refreezing in the snowpack masks high melt extent. Melt-area headlines can overstate actual mass loss in a given year.

insights.claim: Greenland's relatively benign 2026 summer was partly luck. A blocked Omega-shaped jet stream behind heatwaves in southern Europe and North America put Greenland on the cool, wet side. Had the pattern shifted by half a wavelength, Greenland would likely have seen record melt.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Extreme heat in Europe and North America and Greenland's melt share the same atmospheric driver. One placement of the pattern spared Greenland, but tail risk remains in both places.
insights.quote: If the Omega pattern had been displaced by half a wavelength, Greenland would have likely seen warm temperatures that brought record levels of melt

insights.claim: Rising snowfall and rising melt together are consistent with a warming climate, because warmer air holds more water vapour and higher temperatures drive more melt.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Higher snowfall is not evidence against warming. Investors should expect wider swings in both directions rather than a smooth trend.
insights.locator: Increases in both snowfall and melt

insights.claim: On 4 August 2026, an ice island of more than 76 square kilometres and about 150 metres thick broke off Petermann glacier's floating tongue. It was the largest loss of floating ice at Petermann since 2012 and the biggest calving event by any Arctic glacier since 2020.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Large calving events at major outlet glaciers are leading indicators of faster ice discharge from the interior.

insights.claim: Scientists expect two more ice islands, of about 94 and 84 square kilometres, to detach from Petermann glacier as rifts spread. Together with the August 2026 break-off, the three would remove about 22% of Petermann's remaining floating ice.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Floating ice does not raise sea level directly, but Petermann brakes the flow of interior ice to the ocean. Losing it could speed up land-ice discharge, which does raise sea level.

insights.claim: Greenland has recorded net ice loss every year since 1996, in warm, cold and snowy years alike. Thirty years is the period climate scientists typically need to separate a climate signal from natural variability, so mass loss can now be confidently attributed to climate change.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Crossing the standard 30-year attribution threshold removes a common argument against acting on Greenland-driven sea level risk in policy and insurance pricing.
insights.quote: scientists now can confidently say that Greenland mass loss is due to climate change

insights.claim: Greenland's largest single-year loss remains 2012, at about 458bn tonnes. Even the 'quiet' past two years each lost more than 100bn tonnes.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Even the quiet years set a floor of about 100bn tonnes a year of loss, which anchors the baseline for sea level rise.

themes.theme: Sea level and Greenlandification of Antarctica

insights.claim: According to the IMBIE assessment published in Scientific Data, which combines 42 independent estimates, Greenland and Antarctica together lost 11,309bn tonnes of ice between 1979 and 2023. That raised global sea level by about 32mm, and the two ice sheets now account for almost a quarter of observed sea level rise.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Ice sheets are a growing share of sea level rise, which matters for coastal infrastructure, real estate and insurance exposure.

insights.claim: Greenland lost 6,215bn tonnes of ice between 1972 and 2023, an average of 119bn tonnes a year. Two-thirds came from increased discharge and one-third from melt, and annual melt losses accelerated from about 60bn tonnes in the 1980s to 264bn tonnes in the 2010s.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A roughly fourfold rise in melt losses in three decades shows the process is accelerating, not running at a steady rate.

insights.claim: Antarctica lost 4,780bn tonnes of ice, raising sea level by about 13mm. All of that loss came from discharge concentrated in West Antarctica, while East Antarctica stayed relatively stable and even gained a little mass from record snowfall.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Antarctic risk is concentrated in marine-terminating glaciers whose stability is hardest to predict, the main source of uncertainty in sea level projections.

insights.claim: The authors predict the split in sea level contribution will shift toward Antarctica, whose ice sheet is roughly 10 times larger than Greenland's. Processes seen in Greenland for decades, such as surface melt, shrinking sea ice, ice shelf loss and seasonal outlet-glacier retreat, are increasingly appearing in Antarctica, a trend they call 'Greenlandification'.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: If Antarctica follows Greenland's path, long-term sea level rise could be much larger than recent Greenland-dominated trends imply, a major tail risk for coastal assets.
insights.quote: We call this the “Greenlandification” of Antarctica.
